doc.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Favorite sessions: Turrentine's Sugar and Jobim's Stone Flower
summary: Carter picks two albums, noting his ending chord on Sugar and Jobim asking him to find the line.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Uh-hm. Any albums or projects at that time that just still tickle you, that stand out in your mind? Or is it just …

All of them do for different reasons. I'll give two examples and I'll stop. All those that don't get mentioned, they'll get mad at me and they'll probably send me some spam or … flatten my tires. (laughter)

Stanley Turrentine's Sugar. The title tune, Sugar? The last chord is mine. "Stanley, you can end like this, put this chord right here." And that's what we did. And the other record is Storm Flower, Jobim's record, because when I first met him during these sessions, I didn't know. I knew who he was but I never had met him. And not speaking any Portuguese, I was just kind of really over my head, verbally, you know. And he spoke enough English that I felt really silly, you know? So I said, "Mr. Jobim." He said, "Call me Carlos." I said, "What do you want me to do with this?" He said, "Well, I like the way you play from what I hear, and I know you'll find the right notes and the right line to make it work." I said, "Okay, count it off. Let's get this sucker going."
